passage:
Nirmala Masi poured the tea and looked at Gurpreet, who hadn't touched her paratha.
'When I was twenty-five,' she said, 'I was a staff nurse in Ludhiana. I wrote to the matron that expired medicines were being relabelled and used. I did it properly, in writing. Nothing happened. Or rather, something happened to me.
Within a month I was on permanent night duty. My name disappeared from the training list. Someone started saying I was careless with records, that I was bitter because I'd been passed over. People I had shared tiffin with for three years stopped sitting near me in the canteen. Not because they hated me. Because they were scared.
That hurt more than the night shifts, beta. Being made into the problem.'
Gurpreet looked up. 'What did you do?'
'First,' Masi said, 'I stopped believing what they said about me.'

qa.q: Where was Nirmala a staff nurse at twenty-five?
qa.a: She was a staff nurse in Ludhiana.

qa.q: What made young Nirmala feel most hurt?
qa.a: Being made into the problem hurt most: feeling her reputation attacked and friends pulling away out of fear.

qa.q: What turning point does Masi's first step point to at this stage?
qa.a: Refusing to believe the story others told about her protected her sense of self, which she needed before deciding on further steps such as outside advice.

qa.q: What might the colleagues who stopped sitting near Nirmala have been feeling?
qa.a: They were probably scared of being linked to her and targeted too, even if they didn't dislike her.

grounding: It shows, through an aunt's memory, a nurse who raised a concern being sidelined, blamed and avoided by frightened colleagues.

passage:
The power had gone out across the office park, and the HR room was lit only by a laptop screen when Rashmi was called in at 5:40 on Friday.
'Performance concerns,' the HR manager said, sliding a folder across. 'And some feedback about your attitude since March.'
March. The month she had emailed compliance about the invoices.
'My reviews were excellent until March,' Rashmi said.
'This is a transition, not a punishment. Your access ends tonight.'
Outside, rain hammered the glass. Her badge beeped red at the door. In the dim corridor she passed Yash, who had helped her check those invoices. He looked at the floor and kept walking.
Rashmi stood under the dripping porch with her plant and her mug, waiting for an auto that wouldn't come, and felt more ashamed than she had any reason to be.

qa.q: What time was Rashmi called into the HR room?
qa.a: She was called in at 5:40 on Friday.

qa.q: Why does Rashmi feel ashamed even though she did nothing wrong?
qa.a: Being blamed and pushed out makes her feel like the problem, and Yash looking away deepens the hurt.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do next at this stage?
qa.a: She could write down the timeline, including her March email and past reviews, and seek advice from a qualified person or protection body before responding.

qa.q: Why might Yash have looked at the floor?
qa.a: Yash likely fears being targeted too, since he helped check the invoices, and may feel guilty walking past her.

grounding: It shows an employee whose concern was ignored being blamed and pushed out, while a frightened colleague avoids her.
